solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Grumbles, having lost heart in place of battle

indicators.note: losing its heart means the central letter of the word for grumbles goes

parts.note: grumbles means moans, complains

explanation.surface: A soldier complains bitterly, his spirit broken, at the scene of a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost heart' removes A, the middle letter of MOANS.
explanation.definitionFit: Mons in Belgium was the site of a famous 1914 battle, so it is a place of battle by example.

clue.text: Bloke upset having eaten friend's jelly

indicators.note: having eaten means one piece takes another inside it, as food goes inside
upset in a down clue means the word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a bloke is a man
a friend is a pal; the 's is a link meaning has

explanation.surface: An overturned man has swallowed his mate's jelly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses the bloke to give NAM; 'having eaten' then swallows the friend. 'jelly' fairly points to napalm, which is gelled petrol.
explanation.definitionFit: Napalm is jellied petrol used in incendiary weapons, so it is a kind of jelly.

clue.text: Capability, perhaps shown by naughty lap dancers

indicators.note: naughty suggests misbehaving letters, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's ability is displayed by risqué dancers at a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capability' looks like a common noun but is Capability Brown, the great English landscape gardener; 'perhaps' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancelot 'Capability' Brown designed English country parks, an example of a garden designer.

clue.text: Take in sailors, having a ball

parts.note: ABs are able seamen, i.e. sailors
an orb is a ball or sphere

explanation.surface: Welcome some seamen aboard while they enjoy themselves at a dance.
explanation.definitionFit: To absorb is to take in, as a sponge soaks up liquid; a direct synonym.

clue.text: Grey, not half, a lunar ground and made of fine particles

indicators.note: not half means only half the word is kept, the latter half dropped

parts.note: the word grey written out

indicators.note: ground means crushed, so these letters are broken down and rearranged

explanation.surface: Grey moon dust, ground to powder, seems to be made of tiny grains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' leaves GR of GREY; 'ground' rearranges A LUNAR into ANULAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Granular describes a substance consisting of small grains, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Audibly cut the outer surface off fruit

indicators.note: audibly means the word meant is sounded out rather than spelt

parts.note: to pare is to cut away the skin or outer layer

explanation.surface: Peel the skin off a piece of fruit, loudly.
explanation.definitionFit: A pear is a common orchard fruit, an example of the category.

clue.text: Island's city house, no outstandingly impressive thing

parts.note: a lulu is an informal word for something remarkable

explanation.surface: A city on an island has a house that is nothing special after all.
explanation.walkthrough: A LULU is informal for something outstanding, good or bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Honolulu is the capital city on the Hawaiian island of Oahu.

clue.text: 'Arm's things' is wrong — they're 'leg's things'!

indicators.note: is wrong says these letters are in the wrong order and must be rearranged

parts.note: the letters of the phrase, the S of the possessive included

explanation.surface: Someone corrects a slip: those tendons belong to the leg, not the arm.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of 'Arm's' counts as a letter here, giving ten letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The hamstrings are the tendons at the back of the knee, which are indeed parts of the leg.

clue.text: American city given honour — what a surprise!

parts.note: the OM, Order of Merit, is a British honour
aha is an exclamation of surprise or discovery

explanation.surface: A US city receives an award, to general astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: The OM (Order of Merit) is a British honour awarded by the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Omaha is a large city in Nebraska, an example of an American city.

clue.text: Ben and Carol excited by a foreign city

indicators.note: excited suggests agitated letters, so these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ben and Carol are thrilled at the prospect of a trip abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Barcelona is a Spanish city, foreign from a British point of view.

clue.text: This person is indifferent and is trapped

indicators.note: is trapped means the word before is caught inside the other piece

parts.note: so-so means indifferent, middling

explanation.surface: Someone describes a person who is mediocre and also stuck somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' is fodder here, held inside SO-SO by 'is trapped'.
explanation.definitionFit: So-and-so is a stand-in label for an unnamed or unspecified person.

clue.text: Terribly sure? No — inside is very jittery

indicators.note: inside means the following piece goes within the rearranged letters
terribly suggests the words are badly treated, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asked if they are sure says no, they are very anxious inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terribly' makes NEROUS from the first two words; 'inside' then slips the very abbreviation into it. The question-and-answer surface hides that No is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervous means anxious and jumpy, a direct synonym of jittery.

clue.text: Laughable commander? Then take the mickey, not half!

parts.note: CO is commanding officer, a commander

indicators.note: not half means half the word is dropped, keeping only the first half

parts.note: the word mickey written out

explanation.surface: A ridiculous officer is mocked behind his back, and how.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take the mickey' means mock; here 'not half' keeps MIC of MICKEY. 'not half' is also British slang for 'very much'.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic as an adjective means funny or laughable; a direct synonym.

clue.text: Good in Europe perhaps dependent on chance

indicators.note: in means the first piece is placed inside the second

parts.note: Europe is an example of a continent

explanation.surface: Whether things go well across Europe is a matter of luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Contingent means depending on something uncertain, a direct synonym phrase.

clue.text: Rebel troubled about fever brought by bug

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the next piece
troubled suggests disturbed letters, so the word is rearranged

parts.note: ague is an old word for a malarial fever

explanation.surface: A rebel suffering from fever is pestered by an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' makes BELER from the rebel, and 'about' wraps it round the fever. 'bug' looks like an insect but is the verb, to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug is to harass or pester, and to beleaguer is to beset with troubles; synonyms as verbs.

clue.text: A fellow keeping partner outside home is detested

indicators.note: keeping means the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: bod is informal British for a person or fellow

indicators.note: outside means the first piece goes round the second

parts.note: a mate is a partner
in means at home

explanation.surface: A man who keeps his partner out of the house is loathed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' wraps the partner round home to give MINATE, and 'keeping' sets that within the fellow. BOD is British slang for a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Abominated means loathed or hated intensely, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Fresh pulp romances written about — one of our features

parts.note: fresh means new

indicators.note: written about suggests the words are moved about, rearranged

explanation.surface: Trashy love stories have been written up anew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'our' is the newspaper speaking: the Telegraph prints columns.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper column is a regular feature in a daily paper like the one carrying this crossword.

clue.text: Wife and a couple of females sitting on the heather prattling

indicators.note: in a down clue, sitting on means placed above the next piece

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female, twice
ling is a common heather

explanation.surface: A wife and two women sit on the moor chattering away.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'sitting on' puts the first pieces above LING.
explanation.definitionFit: Waffling is talking at length without saying much, a synonym of prattling.

clue.text: Repentant writer, one needing shelter

parts.note: a pen is something that writes
I is the Roman numeral for one
a tent is a shelter

explanation.surface: A sorry author is homeless and needs a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Penitent means feeling sorrow for wrongdoing, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Conclusion sees trendy criminal about to be jailed

parts.note: in means fashionable

indicators.note: to be jailed means the next piece is shut up inside the other

parts.note: a fence is a criminal who receives stolen goods
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: In the end a fashionable crook is locked up for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be jailed' puts the short word for about inside the criminal. In criminal slang a fence receives stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: An inference is a conclusion reached by reasoning, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Cold got by you and me in river — what's the justification?

indicators.note: in means the first pieces are placed inside the next

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
us means you and me

explanation.surface: We both caught a chill in the river, so why were we there?
explanation.walkthrough: The Exe is a river in south-west England, a crossword regular.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse is a reason offered as justification, a synonym.

clue.text: Almost completely enclose old people

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: incase is a variant spelling of encase, to enclose completely

explanation.surface: Elderly people are nearly fenced in.
explanation.definitionFit: The Incas were a pre-Columbian people of Peru, an ancient people.

clue.text: Pet worries saint

parts.note: cares are worries

explanation.surface: Fretting over a holy person's beloved animal.
explanation.definitionFit: To pet is to stroke fondly, and so to caress; synonyms as verbs.

clue.text: Humorous writer, awkward blighter, hard to shake off

indicators.note: awkward suggests clumsy letters, so they are rearranged
to shake off means the named letter is removed

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A comic author is a tiresome nuisance who is difficult to get rid of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to shake off' drops H from BLIGHTER, and 'awkward' rearranges the rest. W. S. Gilbert wrote the comic librettos for Gilbert and Sullivan.
explanation.definitionFit: W. S. Gilbert was a witty Victorian librettist, an example of a humorous writer.

clue.text: Wish for ambassador to be lacking nothing

indicators.note: to be lacking means the named letter is absent from the word

parts.note: an envoy is a diplomatic representative
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Hoping for an ambassador who wants for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To envy is to covet, to wish for what someone else has.

clue.text: Annoyance comes with endless dull work after tea

indicators.note: after means the next piece follows the tea

parts.note: cha is informal British for tea

indicators.note: endless means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a grind is tedious work

explanation.surface: Irritation arrives with a never-ending slog after the tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' turns GRIND into GRIN; CHA is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Chagrin is vexation or annoyance at failure, a synonym.

clue.text: Number seen in Felixstowe!

parts.note: the Suffolk port's name contains the Roman numeral IX in its spelling, so the number is literally visible there

explanation.walkthrough: Felixstowe is a port in Suffolk; look at its letters, not its map: f-e-l-IX-stowe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman numeral IX within the place name stands for this number.

clue.text: Unimportant happenings given no individual broadcasts

parts.note: none means not one, no individual
vents means airs or makes public

explanation.surface: Trivial occurrences that nobody bothers to put on air.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-events are occasions that turn out dull or insignificant, so they are unimportant happenings.

clue.text: German city has only 50% of the things definitely needed

indicators.note: only 50% of means just half the word is kept, the second half dropped

parts.note: essentials are the things that are definitely needed

explanation.surface: A city in Germany has only half of the supplies it really requires.
explanation.walkthrough: 'only 50% of' keeps the first five letters of ESSENTIALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Essen is an industrial city in the Ruhr, an example of a German city.
